Krishna. A central figure in Hindu mythology and an avatar of Vishnu who played a pivotal role in the Mahabharata.

Krishna is revered as both a divine deity and a yogi-prince. He is best known as the charioteer and philosophical guide who delivered the Bhagavad Gita to the warrior prince Arjuna on the battlefield of Kurukshetra.

Krishna is an avatar, an incarnation of Vishnu, appearing on Earth to defeat evil and restore dharma during the age of Dwapara Yuga. Born into royalty, he was raised among cowherd communities, blending divine and earthly experiences in his legendary childhood. This dual nature—at once royal and humble, divine and earthly—defines his unique role in the Hindu pantheon.

He is the central protagonist of the Mahabharata, particularly in the Bhagavad Gita section, where he teaches Arjuna the philosophy of karma yoga and the nature of duty. Krishna is depicted with blue skin, holding a flute, the bansuri, and wearing a peacock feather in his hair. These symbolize divine beauty and enchantment.

Krishna is known for his romantic escapades with the gopis, the cowherd girls, and his eternal love for Radha. These relationships symbolize the soul's devotion to the divine. Yet he also employs both wisdom and cunning in the Mahabharata, orchestrating events to eliminate evil and guide dharma's victory.

He is worshipped in multiple forms: as the cowherd lover, the philosophical teacher, the divine diplomat, and the ultimate sage. His teachings on non-attachment, or nishkama karma, on discipline, and on righteous action remain foundational to Hindu ethics and continue to guide the spiritual lives of millions.
